title: Carried In on Someone's Shoulders
tease: A temple priest throws a stone at a singer who will not move out of the path. That night he is told to go back and carry him in.

source.locus: Divya Sūri Caritam and the Guruparamparā Prabhāvam
source.traditionNote: His own poem, the Amalanādipirāṉ, is ten verses on Raṅganātha's form and contains nothing of the river, the priest or the stone. The episode comes from the hagiographies, and was established by the fourteenth century, when Vedānta Deśika titled his commentary after it.
checkedAgainst: Vedānta Deśika, Munivāhana Bhōgam — his commentary on the poem, named for the episode
S. Palaniappan, 'Hagiography Versus History: The Tamil Pāṇar' (2016), on their actual status in the inscriptions

sourcing.claim: Tiruppāṇāḻvār is the eleventh of the twelve Āḻvārs, of the Pāṇar, who were hereditary musicians
He stood on the far bank of the Kāvēri facing Śrīraṅgam and sang without crossing
He held himself unqualified by birth and kept himself out; nobody drove him away
Lōkasāraṅga Muni, an archaka of the temple, came to the river for water for the Lord's service
He called out, the Āḻvār was too absorbed to respond, and he threw a stone that struck his forehead and drew blood
Blood was found on the forehead of the Raṅganātha image in the same place
Raṅganātha commanded the priest to carry the Āḻvār to the sanctum on his shoulders
The Āḻvār refused on grounds of birth and consented only on learning it was the Lord's command
sourcing.locus: ibid.; Vedānta Deśika's Munivāhana Bhōgam, 'rode reluctantly'

sourcing.claim: Munivāhana — he whose vehicle is a sage — is the Āḻvār's own epithet, not the priest's
His single work is the Amalanādipirāṉ, ten verses describing Raṅganātha from the feet upward, the tenth ending that his eyes will not look at anything else
Vedānta Deśika titled his commentary on the poem the Munivāhana Bhōgam — the Feast of the Sage-Borne One
The Lord told the priest two things: that the stone had struck him, and that he was to carry the singer in; the singer sang nine verses on the way and the tenth before Raṅganātha

variants.differs: Who threw the stone, and whether it was meant
variants.tellings: The standard guruparamparai has the priest throw it himself. One popular telling has him order an assistant to. Some retellings call the hit accidental; the mainstream teaching sites say only that he committed an offence, naming no stone.
variants.weTell: The priest throws it, to move him and not to hurt him. It is attested, and softening it removes the only thing in the story a child can actually recognise.

variants.differs: What happened at the temple that night
variants.tellings: In one telling Raṅganātha appears to the priest in a dream. In another the priest returns to find the gates will not open, and a voice tells him why.
variants.weTell: The Lord speaks to him at the shrine, which is the shorter and more widely told shape.

audience.careNote: A priest throws a stone and cuts a man's head. It is attested and kept, because the point is that he did it without hatred — the singer was simply in the way — and then found out and changed. The exclusion is named as wrong, and nothing is resolved: he is carried in, not walked in.

values: what you do to him you do to me
the rule-keeper is the one who changes

blocks.text: There was a singer called «Tiruppāṇāḻvār», and he stood on the wrong side of the river.
Across the water at Śrīraṅgam was «Raṅganātha», lying asleep on his serpent in the dark of the shrine, and the singer sang to him every day of his life from the far bank and never once crossed over.
Not because a guard stopped him. Because he had been told since he was small that people of his family must not go near it, so often that he believed it, and he kept himself out.
One morning a priest came down to the river for water for the god's bath.
And the singer was standing in the path, with his eyes shut, in the middle of a song.
The priest called out to him to move. He did not hear. The priest called again, and he still did not hear, because he was not there to be called.
So the priest picked up a stone and threw it at him to move him out of the way.
It hit him on the forehead and cut him, and he came out of the song and saw whose path he was standing in, and apologised, and moved.
The priest carried his water up to the temple.
And on the forehead of «Viṣṇu» lying in the dark there was blood, in exactly the place where the stone had gone in.
And the Lord said two things to him. The first was: that was me.
The second was: go back down to the river, and put him on your shoulders, and carry him in here yourself.
So he did. The singer said no, and only agreed when he heard whose instruction it was. And the priest lifted him and carried him the whole way.
He sang nine songs on the road, and the tenth one standing in front of «Raṅganātha» at last.
And the last thing he said was that his eyes had now seen everything they were ever going to want to see.
At Śrīraṅgam, on an island in the «Kāvēri», «Raṅganātha» lies asleep on a serpent in the dark of a very old shrine, and he has been lying there longer than anybody can tell you.
And on the far bank of the river there was a singer.
His name was «Tiruppāṇāḻvār» and he came from the Pāṇar, who were musicians — that was the work of the family, going back as far as the songs did.
He sang to «Raṅganātha» every day of his life. He sang across the water. He never crossed it.
Nobody was standing on the bridge to stop him. That is the part of this that is hard to say properly.
He had been told from the time he was small that people of his family did not go near the temple, because of what they were born into.

He had been told it so often, and so much as though it were a plain fact about the world, that he had taken it inside himself. He kept himself on the far bank, and thought it was the right thing to do.
One morning a priest came down to the river.
His name was Lōkasāraṅga, and he had a job to do — water from the «Kāvēri», carried up for the god's bath, at a particular hour, the way it was done every day.
And there was a man standing in the middle of the path with his eyes shut, singing.
He called out to him to move.
The singer did not hear him, because he was a long way inside a song and not available to be spoken to.
He called again, louder. Nothing.
So he picked up a stone and threw it.
Not to hurt him — to move him, the way you would rap on a table. But a stone is a stone, and it hit the singer on the forehead and opened the skin, and the blood started to come down his face.
What the priest had done is worth getting exactly right, because the whole story turns on it.
The priest did not hate him. He had not woken up that morning wanting to hurt anybody. He simply did not think this man mattered enough to walk around. He was somebody in the way.
And the singer, who was bleeding, apologised. He said he was sorry for having been in the path, and got up, and moved aside, and let the priest go by.
Lōkasāraṅga carried his water up the steps and into the temple and through to the shrine.
And on the forehead of the god lying there in the dark there was blood, fresh, in exactly the place on exactly the side where the stone had gone in.
And «Raṅganātha» said two things to him.
The first was that the stone had hit him. Not his devotee. Him.

The second was an instruction, and it was not an apology to be delivered or a fine to be paid. It was: go back down to the river, and pick that man up, and put him on your shoulders, and carry him in here yourself.
So the priest went back down to the river and found him and told him.
And the singer refused. He said what he had always said, which was that a man like him could not go in there. He only gave way when he understood whose instruction it was.
And then a priest of Śrīraṅgam knelt on the riverbank, took a bleeding musician onto his shoulders, stood up, and carried him through the gates and across the courts and all the way in.

The stone and the shoulders are not in the singer's own poem, which is ten verses long and describes only «Raṅganātha», from his feet upward to his face. The story around it comes from the Śrīvaiṣṇava hagiographies and was firmly established by the fourteenth century, when Vedānta Deśika named his commentary The Feast of the Sage-Borne One.
He sang the whole way. Nine songs between the river and the shrine, and the tenth one standing in front of «Raṅganātha» with nothing at all in between.
The last line of the tenth is that his eyes, having seen this, do not want to look at anything else ever again.

linked.reason: the same wrong on the other side of the country, and there it is the furniture that moves rather than a person

close.question: The priest did not hate him. He just did not think about him. Which of those two is easier to fix?
close.seed: Most of the harm people do is not done on purpose, and that does not make it smaller.

ifTheyAsk.q: Why didn't he just walk in himself?
ifTheyAsk.a: Because he had been told all his life that he must not, and he had come to believe it. That is the saddest part of the story and it is worth saying out loud: he was keeping himself out by then, and he thought it was the right thing to do.

ifTheyAsk.q: Was the priest a bad man?
ifTheyAsk.a: He did a bad thing without meaning to, which is different. He thought the singer was somebody in the way. When he found out what he had really done, he went straight back down to the river — and the story gives him the honour of carrying him.

ifTheyAsk.q: Why carry him instead of letting him walk?
ifTheyAsk.a: That is the question people still ask about this story, and it is a fair one. He is brought in without his feet ever touching the ground, so the old rule is never actually broken. The Lord goes round it rather than through it.
